newsitem.title: GERMANY: Kohl blames opposition for stalling German reforms.
newsitem.headline: Kohl blames opposition for stalling German reforms.

text.p: Chancellor Helmut Kohl blamed the opposition Social Democrats (SPD) on Friday for Germany's slowness to enact tax reforms and said voters would punish them in general elections next year.

Shrugging off his steep slump in opinion polls, Kohl said Germany urgently needed reforms and accused the SPD of "treason" against four million unemployed by stalling his tax restructuring with a veto in the upper house of parliament.

Speaking at a rare news conference in Bonn, Kohl also said the rise of the dollar against the mark was not "earth-shaking". He noted there are often complaints from many of the same quarters when the dollar declines against the mark.
Kohl's off-handed comment sent the dollar slightly higher in foreign exchange markets.

He said the economy's recovery was gathering pace and the unemployment rate of more than 11 percent should begin to fall. He reiterated that Germany would qualify for the single European currency and it would be launched on time in 1999.

Devoting much of the 90-minute briefing to domestic issues, Kohl rebuffed queries about the government's troubles and caustically criticised the SPD, which has pulled well ahead of Kohl's Christian Democrats (CDU) in the polls.
"The voters will see through the tactics of the SPD," Kohl, 67 and chancellor for 15 years, said confidently. He will start his annual holiday in the Austrian Alps shortly.

"They know there is no alternative to our reform course. I am ready to make this argument a central theme of the election campaign. The coalition stands for modernisation and progress, the SPD embodies old thinking and immobility."
Calling his tax reform proposal essential for maintaining Germany's competitive position, Kohl said the capital gains tax had to be eliminated and income tax levels cut sharply.
His centre-right government wants to lower the top rate to 39 percent from 53.

"Our tax reform plans have been endorsed as modern and future-oriented by almost all of the economic experts," Kohl said. "But the SPD is refusing to yield. They think they will have better chances in the election. They are misusing the upper house as a weapon for a total blockade."
SPD chairman Oskar Lafontaine quickly rejected the claims and said Kohl was a spent force whose policies had failed.

"Kohl has again failed to put forth any concrete plans on conquering unemployment," Lafontaine said. "The parties in the governing coalition are deeply split among themselves. Kohl is trying to deflect from his own problems by blaming the SPD."

Kohl said he was willing to seek compromise with the SPD on the tax reform but was ready to use the full power of his position to lash out at the SPD if it continued to wield its blocking majority in the upper house.
"I will not allow these blockade tactics to succeed. If necessary, we will campaign from village to village to spread the word that the SPD is responsible for the standstill."

Kohl said he was not overly concerned about opinion polls that show his coalition falling further behind an alliance of the SPD and the environmental Greens party. He said he had been lagging in the polls many times in the past.
"We are facing a difficult situation at the moment and the people are getting annoyed," Kohl said of the electorate.

"We have a situation similar to the one we had four years ago when the SPD had an 'invincible' candidate," Kohl said of Rudolf Scharping, who was crushed by Kohl in the 1994 election after leading early in the race.

"He's now writing commentaries on the Tour de France," Kohl said before bursting out in laughter. Scharping, a devoted cyclist, is writing a daily column on the French bicycle race for a leading German tabloid, Bild.

"We have a whole year until the next election," Kohl said. "I say, let us wait and see what happens." He later offered a wager of a bottle of wine to one journalist that the opinion polls would be reversed by this time next year.
